draw and label the four cardinal points, practise giving directions to places using the four cardinal points,
use the four compass points to show direction on the interactive map to enrich the mapping skills.
play computer games on the compass direction for enjoyment.
key_inquiry_questions: How can we show direction of places?

Digital Literacy: Learners interact with digital devices as they play computer games on compass direction for enjoyment.
Learning to learn: Learners develop relationships as they share resources and practise giving direction of places using the four cardinal points.
sub_strands.values:
Unity: Learners cooperate as they practise giving direction of places using the four cardinal points.
Respect: Learners show patience as they play computer games on compass direction for enjoyment.
sub_strands.pcis: Creative Thinking: Learners participate in creative games as they play computer games on compass direction for enjoyment.

outcomes.text: identify the four cardinal points of a compass
use the four cardinal points to give directions on a map
appreciate the use of four cardinal points in everyday life

skills.name: Name the four cardinal points, their order and their opposites
skills.mastery: The child names north, east, south and west in order round a compass, knows north is opposite south and east is opposite west, knows that facing north east is on the right hand and west on the left, and knows the sun rises in the east and sets in the west. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the point opposite another
say which side east or west is when facing north
say where the sun rises and sets
find the false step in a learner's answer

skills.name: Give directions between places on a described map
skills.mastery: Given a map described in words or a small table, the child says the direction from one place to another, reverses it correctly and gives the direction a walker faces after a quarter turn. Map questions are in words or a small described table, and any county named on a map is an imaginary one. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say which direction one place lies from another
turn a direction round (A is north of B, so B is south of A)
say the direction after a turn
read a small table of places

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Gives the wrong opposite (thinks the opposite of north is east or west).

example.question: Which point is opposite north on a compass?
example.correct_answer: South

misconceptions.cause: The child reads the four points as a list, not as two straight lines crossing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "East" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw a plus sign: north at the top, south at the bottom, east and west across. Ask for the point straight across.
misconceptions.feedback: North and south are opposite, and east and west are opposite. The opposite point is straight across the compass.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Swaps east and west (thinks that facing north, east is on the left).

example.question: You face north. Which side is east on?
example.correct_answer: The right hand

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures the compass on a page instead of standing in it.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The left hand" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Have the child stand and face north, stretch out the right arm and say "east". Then turn and do it again.
misconceptions.feedback: Face north and east is on your right hand. West is on your left hand.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the sun rises in the west and sets in the east, or rises in the north.

example.question: In which direction does the sun rise?
example.correct_answer: The east

misconceptions.cause: The child remembers the sun being high or low but not the side.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The west" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Watch the sun rise on a school morning and name the side; use it to find east and then the other points.
misconceptions.feedback: The sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives the direction the wrong way round (school is north of the market, so says the market is north of the school).

example.question: A school is north of a market. In which direction is the market from the school?
example.correct_answer: South

misconceptions.cause: The child repeats the word in the sentence and does not turn round to the other place.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "North" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Put two objects on the desk. Ask "from this one to that one", then swap and ask again.
misconceptions.feedback: If the school is north of the market, then the market is south of the school. Turn the direction round.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gets the direction wrong after a turn (facing east and turning left gives south).

example.question: Wanjiku faces east and turns left. Which direction does she face now?
example.correct_answer: North

misconceptions.cause: The child turns the wrong way or does not picture facing the direction.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "South" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Have the child stand and face a wall called east, then turn a quarter turn left and name the new wall.
misconceptions.feedback: Facing east, a turn to the left faces north. A turn to the right would face south.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

sub_strands.sub_strand: Location and size of the County
learning_experiences: brainstorm and list sub-counties in their county,
use relevant print or digital resources to identify the location of the county in relation to neighbouring counties,
discuss the size of the county in relation to the neighbouring counties,
sketch, colour, and display the map of the county in class,
play games on the location of the county in relation to neighbouring counties.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it important to learn the size and location of a county?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital Literacy: Learners develop simple games as they play games on the location of the county in relation to the neighbouring counties
Learning to learn: Learners search for the location and size of their county
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: Learners engage in assigned roles and duties as they discuss the size of the county in relation to the neighbouring counties
sub_strands.pcis:
Problem Solving: Learners play creative games as they locate the county in relation to the neigbouring counties
Effective Communication: Learners brainstorm to identify sub-counties in their county.
sub_strands.links: English: Learners apply listening and speaking skills as they discuss in groups the size of the county in relation to the neigbouring counties

outcomes.text: identify sub-counties in the county
locate the county in relation to neighbouring counties
estimate the size of the county in relation to neighbouring counties
acknowledge the location and size of the county

skills.name: Say what sub-counties are and how they fit inside the county
skills.mastery: The child knows a county is divided into sub-counties and a sub-county into wards, that a sub-county is smaller than its county, and that a neighbouring county is a different county and not one of its sub-counties. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the unit that is part of a county
put county, sub-county and ward in order of size
say whether a place is inside or outside the county
find the false step in a learner's answer

skills.name: Locate the county in relation to its neighbouring counties
skills.mastery: Given a described map or table, the child says which neighbouring county lies in each direction, turns the direction round, and names only the counties that share a boundary, not those further away. Map questions are in words or a small described table, and any county named on a map is an imaginary one. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say which direction a neighbour lies from the county
name the neighbour in a given direction
say which counties share a boundary
read a small table of neighbours

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

skills.name: Compare the size of the county with its neighbours
skills.mastery: Given the areas of counties in square kilometres, the child says which is larger and about how many times, compares the whole numbers by their size and not by their first digit, and does not mix up the size of a county with the number of people in it. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say which county is larger from the areas given
say about how many times larger one is
tell size from population
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a sub-county is bigger than a county.

example.question: Which is bigger, a county or a sub-county?
example.correct_answer: A county

misconceptions.cause: The child knows both names and not which holds the other.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A sub-county" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Use boxes inside boxes: the county box holds several sub-county boxes, which hold wards.
misconceptions.feedback: A county is divided into sub-counties. Many sub-counties make one county, so the county is bigger.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts county, sub-county and ward in the wrong order of size.

example.question: Which is the smallest unit: county, sub-county or ward?
example.correct_answer: Ward

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard the three words but not learned how they nest.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Sub-county" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw the three nested boxes and label them from the outside in; then ask for smallest and largest.
misconceptions.feedback: A county is the biggest. It has sub-counties, and each sub-county has wards. A ward is the smallest.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a neighbouring county is a sub-county of the learner's own county.

example.question: Kalia County has a neighbour called Mwangaza County. Is Mwangaza one of the sub-counties of Kalia?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a sub-county of Kalia
example.correct_answer: No, it is a separate county next to Kalia

misconceptions.cause: The child treats everything nearby as inside the home county.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it is a sub-county of Kalia" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw two county boxes side by side and a boundary line between them; sub-counties are drawn inside one box only.
misconceptions.feedback: A neighbouring county is a different county. Sub-counties are only the parts inside one county.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Reverses the direction of a neighbour.

example.question: On a map, Kitale County lies north of Meru County. In which direction is Meru County from Kitale County?
example.correct_answer: South

misconceptions.cause: The child repeats the word in the sentence and does not turn round.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "North" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Mark two dots on paper and ask the direction from each dot to the other.
misconceptions.feedback: If Kitale lies north of Meru, then Meru lies south of Kitale.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls a county a neighbour when it does not share a boundary with the county.

example.question: Which county is a neighbour of Kalia County, with a shared boundary?
example.correct_answer: The county whose boundary touches Kalia

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks near means next to.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A county two counties away" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Use a described map: trace the boundary of the county and name only the counties that touch it.
misconceptions.feedback: A neighbour shares a boundary with the county. A county with another county between is not a neighbour.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the county with more people is the bigger county.

example.question: County A has 3,000 square kilometres and 900,000 people. County B has 12,000 square kilometres and 400,000 people. Which county is larger in size?
example.wrong_answer: County A, because it has more people
example.correct_answer: County B, because its area is larger

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes up how big a place is with how many people live there.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "County A, because it has more people" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare a large empty field and a small crowded classroom: which has more space and which has more people?
misconceptions.feedback: Size is the area of the land in square kilometres. The number of people tells how crowded it is, not how big it is.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Compares numbers by their first digit instead of their size (thinks 800 is more than 3,000 because 8 is more than 3).

example.question: County A is 800 square kilometres and County B is 3,000 square kilometres. Which is larger?
example.correct_answer: County B

misconceptions.cause: The child looks at the first digit and not at the number of digits.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "County A" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Write the two numbers in a place value table and compare the thousands first.
misconceptions.feedback: Compare the whole numbers. 3,000 is more than 800, so County B has the larger area.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: brainstorm the main physical features in the county, sketch the main physical features in the county,
draw or take photographs of the main physical features in the county,
outline the importance of the main physical features in the county and share the discussion points in class,
display pictures or models of the main physical features in the county in class,
find out from parents or guardians the main physical features in the county and share.
key_inquiry_questions: Which physical features are found in your county?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Citizenship: Learners identify the main physical features in their county.
Learning to: Learners find out from parents or guardians the physical features in the county and share
sub_strands.values: Social Justice: Learners accord equal opportunities in sharing responsibilities as they outline the importance of the main physical features in the county and share the discussion points in class.
sub_strands.pcis: Self-Awareness: Learners appreciate each other’s abilities as they draw some of the main physical features in the county.
sub_strands.links: English: Learners use speaking skills as they discuss in groups the importance of the main physical features in the county in class.

outcomes.text: identify the main physical features in the county
state the importance of the main physical features in the county
illustrate the main physical features in the county
appreciate the main physical features in the county

skills.name: Identify the main kinds of physical feature in a county
skills.mastery: The child names a hill (low rounded high ground), a mountain (much higher), a valley (low land between hills or mountains), a plain (wide flat land), a river (water flowing in a channel), a lake (water with land around it) and the ocean coast from a short description. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the kind of feature from a description
pick the odd one out
tell a hill from a mountain, a river from a lake, a plain from a valley
find the false step in a learner's answer

skills.name: State how physical features help people
skills.mastery: The child matches rivers and lakes to water, fish and irrigation, mountains and hills to rain, forests and tourism, plains to farming and building, and the coast to fishing and ports, and does not call a feature useless or give it a use it does not have. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: match a feature to its use
say why a feature matters to the people near it
pick the false use
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a hill and a mountain are the same or a hill is higher.

example.question: Which is higher, a hill or a mountain?
example.correct_answer: A mountain

misconceptions.cause: The child uses the two words for any raised ground.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A hill" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare Mount Kenya with a small hill near school: describe the height of each.
misconceptions.feedback: A mountain is much higher than a hill. A hill is lower and usually rounded.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up a river and a lake.

example.question: Which one is water that flows along in a channel?
example.correct_answer: A river

misconceptions.cause: The child knows both have water.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A lake" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: does the water stay in one place or move on to the sea or a lake?
misconceptions.feedback: A river flows along a channel. A lake is water that stays in a hollow, with land all round it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up a plain and a valley (thinks a valley is wide flat land).

example.question: Which is wide flat land?
example.correct_answer: A plain

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks low land is flat land.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A valley" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a bowl and a flat table: a valley lies between high land on both sides, a plain is wide and flat.
misconceptions.feedback: A plain is wide, flat land. A valley is low land between hills or mountains.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks physical features have no use for people (only beautiful).

example.question: Why is a river important to people near it?
example.wrong_answer: It is only nice to look at
example.correct_answer: It gives water for drinking, farming and fish

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the features as scenery.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is only nice to look at" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask each learner to name one thing in the day that comes from water or land near home.
misconceptions.feedback: Physical features are useful. Rivers give water and fish, mountains bring rain and visitors, plains give farmland.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Matches a feature to a use it does not have (farming on a lake, fishing on a plain).

example.question: Which feature is best for fishing?
example.correct_answer: A lake

misconceptions.cause: The child guesses from the word and not from what the feature is.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A plain" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Match each feature to what it is made of: water, high ground, flat land. Then ask what each can give.
misconceptions.feedback: Fish live in water, so lakes, rivers and the sea give fish. Plains are flat dry land, good for farming.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks mountains and valleys only get in the way and do no good.

example.question: How does a mountain help people?
example.correct_answer: It brings rain, rivers and visitors

misconceptions.cause: The child sees only the difficulty of travelling over a mountain.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It only blocks the road" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Trace a river from its source on a mountain to the farms below.
misconceptions.feedback: Mountains help us. Rain falls on them and feeds rivers, they grow tea and trees, and visitors come to climb them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: brainstorm about seasons experienced in the county,
use print or digital resources to identify seasons experienced in the county
engage a resource person to find out how seasons influence human activities in the county
discuss ways in which rainy weather affects safety of road users,
draw weather charts of seasons in the county,
observe and record in charts human activities associated with different seasons.
sing songs about seasons experienced in the county,
key_inquiry_questions: How do seasons influence human activities in the county?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Collaboration: Learners develop relationships as they brainstorm about seasons experienced in the county.
Digital Literacy: Learners use print or digital resources to identify seasons experienced in the county.
sub_strands.values:
Respect: Learners appreciate diverse opinions as they brainstorm about seasons experienced in the county.
Patriotism: Learners sing songs about seasons experienced in the county,
sub_strands.pcis: Safety and security: Learners discuss precautions to take during the different seasons experienced in the county (Hot, cold, dry and rainy season).
sub_strands.links: Agriculture: Learners explain how different seasons influence human activities in the county.

outcomes.text: identify the four seasons experienced in the county
explain how the four seasons influence human activities in the county
explore how rainy weather affects road safety in the county
model weather charts of seasons in the county
appreciate the different seasons experienced in the county

skills.name: Name the four seasons of the county and tell them apart
skills.mastery: The child names the four seasons as hot, cold, dry and rainy, matches each to its weather, knows the long rains come around March to May and the short rains around October to December, and does not use the names spring, summer, autumn and winter or call one rainy day a season. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the season from its weather
pick the season that has long or short rains
say whether a statement is about one day or a whole season
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: Grade 3 Environmental Activities taught the idea first. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

skills.name: Explain how the seasons change what people do
skills.mastery: The child says farmers plant when the rains begin and harvest and dry crops in the dry season, that people wear warm clothes in the cold season and drink and sell cold drinks in the hot season, and that the seasons do change what people do. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the activity that suits a season
say what a farmer does in a season
say what people wear or sell in a season
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

skills.name: Say how rainy weather affects road safety and choose safe behaviour
skills.mastery: The child says rain makes roads slippery, muddy and sometimes flooded and makes it harder to see, that a driver must slow down, and that a person must never cross flooded water, never run across a road, and wait in a safe place. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: say what rain does to a road
choose the safe thing to do near a flooded road
say what a driver should do in heavy rain
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
Grade 3 Environmental Activities taught the idea first. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses spring, summer, autumn and winter as the seasons of the county.

example.question: Which of these is a season in our county?
example.correct_answer: The rainy season

misconceptions.cause: The child has met the four names in picture books from other lands.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Autumn" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask the child to name the weather of each month of the school year, then give each stretch its own name.
misconceptions.feedback: Our seasons are hot, cold, dry and rainy. Autumn and winter belong to places far from the equator.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up the seasons (thinks the rainy season is the hot season, or cold means rain).

example.question: When there is little rain and no clouds for many days, which season is it?
example.correct_answer: The dry season

misconceptions.cause: The child names a season by one feature and not by the whole.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The rainy season" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Make a weather chart over a week and name the season from what it shows.
misconceptions.feedback: No rain for many days is the dry season. Long rains come about March to May and short rains about October to December.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Treats one day of weather as a whole season.

example.question: It rained on Tuesday. What can we say?
example.wrong_answer: It is now the rainy season
example.correct_answer: It rained that day, and a season lasts for many weeks

misconceptions.cause: The child does not tell weather of a day from a season.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is now the rainy season" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the weather was every day of one month, then name the season.
misconceptions.feedback: One rainy day is weather. A season is the weather that comes for many weeks, month after month.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks farmers should plant when the ground is dry.

example.question: When do farmers plant maize?
example.correct_answer: When the rains begin

misconceptions.cause: The child does not link the seeds to the need for water.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "In the dry season" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Plant two cups of beans, water one, and compare after a week.
misconceptions.feedback: Farmers plant when the rains begin, so that the seeds get water. They harvest and dry the crop in the dry season.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Matches a season to an activity that does not fit it (warm sweaters in the hot season).

example.question: What do people wear in the cold season?
example.correct_answer: Warm clothes such as sweaters

misconceptions.cause: The child does not think of the weather of the season.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Light cotton shirts only" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the child wears on a cold morning and what on a hot afternoon.
misconceptions.feedback: In the cold season people wear sweaters and jackets. In the hot season they wear light clothes.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks seasons make no difference to what people do.

example.question: Do seasons change what people do?
example.wrong_answer: No, people do the same all year
example.correct_answer: Yes, farmers, traders and travellers change what they do

misconceptions.cause: The child lives in a town and does not see farming.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, people do the same all year" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what changes at home when the rains start: crops, roads, clothes, school trips.
misconceptions.feedback: Seasons change many things: when farmers plant and harvest, what people wear, sell and how they travel.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks it is safe to run across a wet road to get out of the rain.

example.question: It is raining. What should Njeri do at the road?
example.wrong_answer: Run across fast to get out of the rain
example.correct_answer: Wait at the side and cross only when the road is clear

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of being dry, not of slippery roads and poor sight.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Run across fast to get out of the rain" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Role play crossing in the rain: slow, look both ways, hold a friend's hand.
misconceptions.feedback: Never run across a road. Rain makes roads slippery and drivers cannot see well. Wait and cross when it is clear.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks it is safe to cross flooded water if it looks shallow.

skills.name: Describe how people are spread over a county and the reasons

Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up population distribution with the total number of people.

example.question: What does population distribution mean?
example.wrong_answer: The total number of people in a county
example.correct_answer: How people are spread over an area

misconceptions.cause: The child links "population" with counting.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The total number of people in a county" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Place twelve counters on a page: first all in one corner, then spread out; the total is the same.
misconceptions.feedback: Distribution is how people are spread over the area. The total number is a different thing.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a dense area is a large area.

example.question: An area has many people living close together. Is it dense or sparse?
example.correct_answer: Dense

misconceptions.cause: The child links dense with large size or fills the word with a different meaning.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Sparse" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare ten learners in a small room and ten on a football pitch.
misconceptions.feedback: Dense means many people in a small space. Sparse means few people spread over a large space.

misconceptions.feedback: People live where they can get water, food, work, roads and safety. Dry, steep, flooded or unsafe places have few people.

example.correct_answer: Farmers, workers, traders and everyone who eats

misconceptions.cause: The child links activity to the wealth of the owner.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only rich people" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Trace a loaf of bread from the farm to the table and name the people who gain at each step.
misconceptions.feedback: Many people gain: the farmer, the worker, the trader and every person who buys food.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks activities give only food, not jobs, income or raw materials.

example.question: Which is a reason that mining matters to a county?
example.correct_answer: It gives jobs, income and raw materials

misconceptions.cause: The child gives the answer for farming to every activity.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It gives food" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Make a table of five activities and what each gives.
misconceptions.feedback: Activities give jobs, income and raw materials, and some give food. Mining gives jobs and minerals.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Identify industries by what they make from what
skills.mastery: The child says an industry makes or processes goods from raw materials (milk to packed milk, sugarcane to sugar, tea leaves to tea, maize to flour), keeps raw material and product the right way round, and does not call a shop or a farm an industry. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

say what an industry does to a raw material
say whether a place is an industry
find the false step in a learner's answer

skills.name: Explain the benefits of industries in a county
skills.mastery: The child says industries give jobs, income, a market for farmers, goods to buy and money for the county, and says the benefits reach workers, farmers and shoppers, not only the owner. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

say who gains from a factory
say what happens to farmers near a factory
find the false step in a learner's answer

skills.mastery: Given a described map or table, the child places an industry near its raw material, workers, roads and water and reads where an industry is from the table. Map questions are in words or a small described table, and any county named on a map is an imaginary one. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the best place for an industry
read where an industry is from a small table
say why an industry is near its raw material or market
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.
This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Swaps the raw material and the product (thinks sugar is the raw material for sugarcane).

example.question: What is the raw material in a sugar factory?
example.correct_answer: Sugarcane

misconceptions.cause: The child names the thing he or she knows best.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Sugar" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Use pairs: before the factory and after the factory.
misconceptions.feedback: The raw material goes in. Sugarcane goes into the factory and sugar comes out.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls a shop or a farm an industry.

example.question: Which place is an industry?
example.correct_answer: A factory that turns sugarcane into sugar

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks any busy business is an industry.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A shop that sells sugar" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: does this place make something new from something else?
misconceptions.feedback: An industry makes or processes goods. A shop only sells goods and a farm grows the raw materials.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only the owner gains from an industry.

example.question: Who gains when a factory opens in a county?
example.correct_answer: Workers, farmers, shoppers and the county

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the owner as the only person involved.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only the owner" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List who works at a milk factory, who sells it the milk and who buys the milk.
misconceptions.feedback: Workers get jobs, farmers get a market, shoppers get goods and the county gets money.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Lists pollution or noise as a benefit.

example.question: Which is a benefit of an industry?
example.correct_answer: Jobs for people in the county

misconceptions.cause: The child does not tell a benefit from a problem.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Dirty smoke from the chimney" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sort a list into "good for people" and "problem to solve".
misconceptions.feedback: Jobs, income and goods are benefits. Smoke and waste are problems that industries must control.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks an industry can be built anywhere with no reason.

example.question: Why is a sugar factory built near sugarcane farms?
example.wrong_answer: Because there is no reason, any place does
example.correct_answer: Because the heavy cane is cheap to carry a short way

misconceptions.cause: The child does not link the place to the cost or ease of work.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Because there is no reason, any place does" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask the child to carry a heavy bag a short way and a long way.
misconceptions.feedback: Factories are placed near raw materials, workers, roads, water and a market, so that costs are lower.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Places an industry far from its raw material (a milk factory far from dairy farms).

example.question: Where is the best place for a milk factory?
example.correct_answer: Near the dairy farms, with good roads

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks only about the buyer, not about milk that goes bad.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Far from any dairy farms" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what happens to fresh milk after a day in the sun.
misconceptions.feedback: Milk goes bad quickly, so the factory is near the farms, on a good road.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Choose enterprise projects a school can start
skills.mastery: The child names school projects (kitchen garden, poultry, tree nursery, bee-keeping, making liquid soap, recycling), chooses the one that suits the land, water and people the school has, and knows a project needs a plan. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the project that suits the school's resources
say what a project needs before it starts
say what a project earns or gives
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

skills.name: Say what honest and shared work means in a school project
skills.mastery: The child says project money is kept honestly and recorded, the team shares the work and decisions, mistakes are reported, and profit belongs to the project and school, not to one person. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the honest action with project money
say how the team should work
say what to do with a mistake or a loss
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Chooses a project that needs what the school does not have (fish ponds with no water).

example.question: A school has a dry field and no water tank. Which project suits it best?
example.correct_answer: Keeping bees or planting drought-resistant trees

misconceptions.cause: The child picks the most exciting project and does not check what is needed.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Fish farming" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List what each project needs and tick what the school has.
misconceptions.feedback: Choose a project that suits your land, water, money and people. Fish need water.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a project needs no plan, just start.

example.question: What should a school do before starting a project?
example.wrong_answer: Start at once with no plan
example.correct_answer: Make a plan of work, materials and who does what

misconceptions.cause: The child links enterprise with action only.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Start at once with no plan" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Plan a class lunch together: who brings what, and what does it cost?
misconceptions.feedback: A project needs a plan: what to do, the materials, the people, the cost and the time.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a leader can keep the money the project makes.

example.question: The class sold vegetables and made 500 shillings. What should the treasurer do?
example.correct_answer: Record it and keep it safely for the project

misconceptions.cause: The child sees money as belonging to whoever holds it.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Keep it for himself" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Role play the treasurer with a record book and a locked box.
misconceptions.feedback: Project money belongs to the project and the school. Keep it safe and record every shilling.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a mistake or a loss should be hidden to avoid blame.

example.question: A group loses some money by mistake. What is right?
example.wrong_answer: Hide it so no one is blamed
example.correct_answer: Report it honestly and learn from it

misconceptions.cause: The child fears blame.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Hide it so no one is blamed" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Practise saying "we lost it, and here is what we will do".
misconceptions.feedback: Honest groups report their mistakes and lose less over time. Hiding them breaks trust.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks one strong leader should do all the work or decide everything.

example.question: How should a project team decide?
example.correct_answer: The team shares ideas and decides together

misconceptions.cause: The child sees leadership as control.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The leader decides everything alone" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask the team to decide where to keep the tools, then compare it with one person deciding.
misconceptions.feedback: Teams share the work and the decisions, so everyone takes part and feels the project belongs to them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

role-play qualities of a good citizen in a school,

sub_strands.links: English: Learners apply writing skills as they write an essay on a good digital citizen (using technology in a positive way) and share the essays in class.

outcomes.text: identify qualities of a good citizen in school
develop qualities of good citizenship in school
appreciate qualities of good citizenship in school

skills.name: Identify the qualities of a good citizen in school
skills.mastery: The child names the qualities of a good school citizen (respect, honesty, responsibility, obedience to fair rules, helping others, keeping the school clean, being on time, caring for property) and does not say that only the top learners or those who never speak are good citizens. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the quality in a situation
pick the action of a good citizen
say whether a statement about good citizens is true
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only learners with the top marks are good citizens.

example.question: Who is a good citizen in school?
example.wrong_answer: Only the learner with the top marks
example.correct_answer: Any learner who is respectful, honest and helpful

misconceptions.cause: The child links a good learner with good marks.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only the learner with the top marks" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what a learner can do for others even with low marks.
misconceptions.feedback: A good citizen shows qualities such as respect, honesty and helpfulness. Marks are different from character.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a good citizen only keeps quiet and obeys, never speaks up.

example.question: Which learner is a good citizen?
example.correct_answer: The one who keeps fair rules and helps others, and speaks up kindly when something is wrong

misconceptions.cause: The child links good with silent.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The one who never speaks" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Role play a learner who sees someone bullied: what is the good action?
misconceptions.feedback: A good citizen follows fair rules, cares for others, and politely speaks up when something is wrong.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks telling a teacher about bullying is wrong (telling tales).

example.question: You see a learner being bullied. What does a good citizen do?
example.wrong_answer: Say nothing, because telling tales is wrong
example.correct_answer: Tell a teacher and help the learner

misconceptions.cause: The child confuses reporting harm with gossip.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Say nothing, because telling tales is wrong" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: is it gossip to tell a teacher that someone is being hurt?
misconceptions.feedback: Telling a teacher about harm is not telling tales. A good citizen helps keep everyone safe.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Identify the things that promote peace in school
skills.mastery: The child says respect, sharing, honesty, listening, fairness, forgiveness and accepting differences promote peace, and that peace means disagreements are settled without hurting anyone, not that nobody ever disagrees. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick what promotes peace
pick what breaks peace
say what peace means
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

skills.name: Choose ways of settling a quarrel peacefully
skills.mastery: The child chooses to stay calm, listen, talk it through, say sorry and forgive, and to ask a teacher or peer mediator for help, and does not choose to fight back, take revenge or gossip. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the peaceful way to react
put the steps of settling a quarrel in order
say who can help
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks peace means nobody ever disagrees.

example.question: What does peace mean in school?
example.correct_answer: Settling disagreements without hurting anyone

misconceptions.cause: The child sees peace as quiet.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nobody ever disagrees" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask for a time when two friends disagreed and still stayed friends.
misconceptions.feedback: People will sometimes disagree. Peace is settling it with respect and without harm.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks peace comes from fear and punishment.

example.question: What keeps a school peaceful?
example.correct_answer: Respect, fairness and listening

misconceptions.cause: The child links order with punishment.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Fear of strict punishment" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare a class that is quiet for the cane and a class that is kind by choice.
misconceptions.feedback: Peace grows from respect, fairness, sharing and forgiveness, not from fear.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks spreading talk about others or taking sides helps peace.

example.question: Which action breaks peace?
example.correct_answer: Spreading rumours about a classmate

misconceptions.cause: The child does not see how talk hurts.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Listening to both sides" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Pass a message along a line and watch it change.
misconceptions.feedback: Rumours and name-calling break peace. Listening, honesty and kind words keep it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks hitting back or revenge settles a quarrel.

example.question: A classmate pushes you by mistake. What is the peaceful reply?
example.correct_answer: Stay calm and say what happened

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks strength ends a quarrel.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Push back harder" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Role play both: what happens after a push back, and after a calm word?
misconceptions.feedback: Hitting back makes a quarrel bigger. Stay calm, talk, and ask a teacher to help if needed.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks pretending the problem is not there is the best way, and never speaking again.

example.question: Two friends quarrelled. What is the best way to settle it?
example.wrong_answer: Never speak to each other again
example.correct_answer: Talk about it, say sorry and forgive

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks silence ends a quarrel.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Never speak to each other again" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask how the friendship feels after a week of silence.
misconceptions.feedback: Silence does not settle a quarrel. Talk, listen, say sorry and forgive.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts the steps of settling a quarrel in the wrong order (apologise before listening).

example.question: What comes first when settling a quarrel?
example.wrong_answer: Shout until the other gives in
example.correct_answer: Calm down and listen

misconceptions.cause: The child does not think of steps.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Shout until the other gives in" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Write the steps on cards and order them: calm, listen, talk, say sorry, forgive.
misconceptions.feedback: First calm down and listen. Then talk about it, say sorry and forgive. A mediator can help.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.mastery: The child names effects (injury, fear, sadness, dropping out of school, poor health), says a child who is hurt or whose friend is hurt must tell a trusted adult such as a teacher, parent or the Childline helpline on 116, and says harm is not kept secret. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick an effect of child abuse
say what a child should do who is being hurt
say what a child should do when a friend is hurt
find the false step in a learner's answer

misconceptions.error: Thinks beating a child is only discipline and never abuse.

example.question: A teacher beats a learner until he is hurt. Is this child abuse?
example.correct_answer: Yes, hurting a child is abuse

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen beating treated as normal.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, it is only discipline" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: does discipline teach with care or hurt? Discuss other ways, such as talking and fair consequences.
misconceptions.feedback: Hurting a child is abuse. Discipline teaches without harming the child.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks any work a child does is fine (or that all chores are child labour).

example.question: Which is child labour?
example.correct_answer: Working all day in a quarry instead of going to school

misconceptions.cause: The child does not tell light chores from harmful work.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Washing a plate after supper" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sort examples by: safe, short, does not stop school, does not harm.
misconceptions.feedback: Light chores that do not stop school or harm the child are fine. Heavy or dangerous work that stops school is child labour.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only beating counts as child abuse.

example.question: Which of these is child abuse?
example.correct_answer: Forcing a girl to marry early

misconceptions.cause: The child knows only the form seen most often.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only beating a child" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List six forms and ask: how does each harm the child?
misconceptions.feedback: Child abuse takes many forms: forced marriage, labour, trafficking, neglect and sexual abuse, as well as beating.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a child causes the abuse by bad behaviour.

example.question: Why was a child abused by an adult?
example.correct_answer: The adult chose to harm the child

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard "you made me do it".
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The child behaved badly" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: can anything a child does make it right for an adult to hurt him or her?
misconceptions.feedback: Abuse is never the child's fault. The adult is responsible for the harm.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a custom or tradition makes an abuse acceptable.

example.question: Some say a harmful custom is fine because it is old. What is right?
example.wrong_answer: It is fine if it is a tradition
example.correct_answer: A custom that harms a child must stop

misconceptions.cause: The child respects elders and customs.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is fine if it is a tradition" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Discuss that culture changes, and that keeping children safe is also a tradition.
misconceptions.feedback: No custom makes harm to a child right. Many customs are good, but harmful ones must stop.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks children forget abuse and are not changed by it.

example.question: What can child abuse do to a child?
example.correct_answer: It can hurt the body, cause fear and make the child leave school

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks harm only shows on the body.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing, children forget" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List ways a bad experience at school changes how a learner feels.
misconceptions.feedback: Abuse can injure, frighten and make a child sad, sick or leave school.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a hurt child or a friend should keep it secret.

example.question: A friend tells you an adult is hurting him. What should you do?
example.correct_answer: Tell a trusted adult such as a teacher, or call Childline on 116

misconceptions.cause: The child fears trouble or being a tell-tale.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Keep it a secret" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Make a list of the adults who keep children safe and practise saying "I need to tell you something".
misconceptions.feedback: Never keep harm secret. Tell a trusted adult, or call Childline on 116, which is free.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

explain the benefits of democracy in school

skills.name: Identify democratic processes in school
skills.mastery: The child says democratic processes in school include electing prefects by a secret vote, class meetings, debates and suggestion boxes, puts the election steps in order (nomination, campaign, voting, counting, announcing) and knows a teacher appointing someone is not an election. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the democratic way to choose
put the steps of a school election in order
say whether a way of choosing is democratic
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

skills.name: Explain the benefits of democracy in school
skills.mastery: The child says democracy gives everyone a voice, is fair, builds peace, and makes decisions that most learners accept, and that the choice of the majority is followed while the views of the others are still respected. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick a benefit of democracy
say what the majority and the minority each get
say why everyone should vote
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a leader chosen by the teacher is an election.

example.question: Which way of choosing a head prefect is democratic?
example.correct_answer: All learners vote

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks any choosing is an election.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The teacher picks a favourite" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare: who chose? how many people had a say?
misconceptions.feedback: In an election all voters have a say. A teacher choosing alone is appointing.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts election steps in the wrong order (voting before the campaign).

example.question: Which comes first in a school election?
example.correct_answer: Nominating the candidates

misconceptions.cause: The child remembers voting and counting only.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Counting the votes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Order the steps on cards: nominate, campaign, vote, count, announce.
misconceptions.feedback: The order is nomination, campaign, voting, counting and announcing the winner.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the loudest or most popular learner wins by right.

example.question: How should a winner be decided?
example.correct_answer: By counting the votes of everyone

misconceptions.cause: The child links winning with being strong.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The loudest learner wins" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Hold a vote on a class song and count each hand.
misconceptions.feedback: The winner is the candidate with the most votes, counted fairly.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks those who lose a vote have no say and no value.

example.question: After a vote, what happens to the views of those who lost?
example.correct_answer: They are still respected

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the vote as a win or loss only.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "They are ignored" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: After a class vote, ask the losers to say one idea that could still be used.
misconceptions.feedback: The majority choice is followed, but everyone's views are respected.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks democracy wastes time and one person should decide.

example.question: Why is democracy good for a school?
example.wrong_answer: It is not, one person is quicker
example.correct_answer: It gives everyone a voice and is fair

misconceptions.cause: The child values speed over fairness.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is not, one person is quicker" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare a lunch menu chosen by one person with one chosen by the class.
misconceptions.feedback: Democracy gives everyone a voice, is fair and builds peace, even if it takes a little time.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Say who is in the Children's Government and how they are chosen
skills.mastery: The child says the Children's Government is made up of learners elected by their classmates, with a leader and ministers or prefects for different areas, guided by a patron teacher, and not by teachers alone. Posts and names vary by school. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick who belongs to the Children's Government
say how members are chosen
say who guides the learners
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

skills.name: Describe what the Children's Government does
skills.mastery: The child says the Children's Government speaks for learners, helps keep order and cleanliness, organises school activities and passes learners' worries to the teachers, and does not punish learners or run the school in place of the head teacher. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick a duty of the Children's Government
pick what it does not do
say who a learner takes a worry to
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the Children's Government is made up of teachers.

example.question: Who forms the Children's Government?
example.correct_answer: Learners elected by their classmates

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks anything with "government" belongs to adults.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The teachers" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask who voted for last year's prefects.
misconceptions.feedback: The Children's Government is made of learners chosen by learners, with a teacher patron to guide them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the head teacher alone appoints all members.

example.question: How are members of the Children's Government chosen?
example.wrong_answer: The head teacher picks them all
example.correct_answer: Learners vote for them

misconceptions.cause: The child has not seen the election.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The head teacher picks them all" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Walk through one election: nomination, campaign, vote.
misconceptions.feedback: Learners vote for their leaders, so that the leaders speak for them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the Children's Government can punish or cane learners.

example.question: Which is NOT a duty of the Children's Government?
example.correct_answer: Passing learners' worries to the teachers

misconceptions.cause: The child links prefects with punishing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Caning learners who are late" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what a prefect can do kindly: remind, report, help.
misconceptions.feedback: The Children's Government helps keep order but does not punish. Teachers handle punishment.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks it runs the school in place of the head teacher.

example.question: Who runs the school?
example.correct_answer: The head teacher and the school management

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks leaders have the power of the head.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The Children's Government" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw who reports to whom.
misconceptions.feedback: The Children's Government speaks for learners and helps. The head teacher runs the school.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Identify leaders in the community and their duties

Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

say what a leader does
pick the odd one out
find the false step in a learner's answer

skills.name: Choose the qualities of a good leader in the community
skills.mastery: The child says a good leader is honest, fair, listens, serves everyone and sets an example, and does not say a leader is good because he or she is the strongest, the richest or the loudest. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the quality of a good leader
say how a good leader acts in a situation
say why leaders must be honest
find the false step in a learner's answer

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks leaders are only politicians.

example.question: Which is a leader in the community?
example.correct_answer: A village elder, a religious leader or the chief

misconceptions.cause: The child hears "leader" mainly in the news.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only a politician" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask who helps settle problems in the village.
misconceptions.feedback: Leaders in the community include religious leaders, clan leaders, village elders and the chief.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives a leader the wrong duty (the chief counsels in worship).

example.question: Who guides people in faith and prayer?
example.correct_answer: A religious leader

misconceptions.cause: The child knows the names but not the duties.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The chief" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Match each leader to the duty on a chart.
misconceptions.feedback: Religious leaders guide in faith, elders settle disputes and the chief keeps law and order.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the strongest or richest person is the best leader.

example.question: Which person would make a good leader?
example.correct_answer: The honest person who listens

misconceptions.cause: The child links power with leading.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The richest person" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask which classmate you would follow and why.
misconceptions.feedback: A good leader is honest, fair and listens. Strength and wealth do not make a leader good.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks leaders can use their post to benefit themselves.

misconceptions.help: Discuss why trust matters to a leader.
misconceptions.feedback: A good leader serves everyone and is honest with what belongs to the community.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Identify the structure of the county government
skills.mastery: The child says a county government has a county executive (the Governor, the Deputy Governor and the county executive committee members) and a county assembly (the Members of the County Assembly and the Speaker), and does not mix it up with the President and Members of Parliament. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

find the false step in a learner's answer

skills.name: Explain the duties of the County Governor
skills.mastery: The child says the Governor is elected by the people of the county for five years, heads the county executive, sees that county laws are carried out, appoints the county executive committee with the assembly's approval and reports on the county, and does not make laws or head the country. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick a duty of the Governor
pick what the Governor does not do

find the false step in a learner's answer

skills.name: Explain the roles of a Member of the County Assembly
skills.mastery: The child says a Member of the County Assembly (MCA) is elected by a ward, makes county laws, approves the county budget, checks the work of the executive and speaks for the people of the ward, and does not carry out the laws or speak for the whole country. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick a duty of the MCA
say whom an MCA represents
pick what an MCA does not do
find the false step in a learner's answer

misconceptions.error: Mixes county government with national government (puts the President and MPs in the county).

misconceptions.cause: The child hears the names on the news and puts them all together.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The President" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.

misconceptions.error: Puts the Governor in the county assembly or the MCAs in the executive.

indicators.indicator: Ability to identify qualities of good citizenship in school

levels.EE: Learner identifies qualities of good citizenship in school with examples
levels.ME: Learner identifies qualities of good citizens in school
levels.AE: Learner identifies some qualities of good citizens in school
levels.BE: Learner has challenges identifying the qualities of good citizens in school

indicators.indicator: Ability to develop strategies of living in peace with others in school

levels.EE: Learner develops strategies of living in peace with others in school citing with examples
levels.ME: Learner develops strategies of living in peace with others in school
levels.AE: Learner develops some strategies of living in peace with others in school
levels.BE: Learner has challenges developing strategies of living in peace with others in school

indicators.indicator: Ability to explain effects of the seven forms of child abuse in the community

levels.EE: Learner explains effects of the seven forms of child abuse in the community with examples
levels.ME: Learner explains effects of the seven forms of child abuse in the community
levels.AE: Learner explains effects of 4-6 forms of child abuse in the community
levels.BE: Learner explains effects of less than 4 forms of child abuse in the community
